subject.title: San Francisco Board of Supervisors, District 10

positions.statement: "Supervisor, D10 - Pearci 'PJ' Bastiany III" / "PJ Bastiany is a martial artist and community organizer who is running a campaign in support of affordable housing, safety, and opportunity in District 10. We awarded him our sole endorsement." / "Although he's a member of the Democratic Party, Bastiany is a fierce opponent of the Israeli genocide in Gaza. He became a supporter of Green Party gubernatorial candidate Butch Ware due to Ware's outspoken advocacy for Palestinians. Bastiany also shares a number of other Green Values, including strong support for housing that is truly affordable to current members of the community, as well as an emphasis on creative, community-based public safety measures as an alternative to simply throwing more money at the police. He also supports a rollback of 'care not cash' to give assistance directly to people in need." / "Although he's been excluded from coverage by mainstream press outlets (including Mission Local), we think Bastiany is an exciting candidate and we look forward to hearing more of his ideas in the future. We award him our sole endorsement."

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition I (Changes to Real Property Transfer Tax)

positions.statement: "no consensus for or against I - dedicate $120 million from real estate transfer tax to 'affordable housing'" / "Prop I would make changes to the real estate transfer tax (2020's Prop I), which we strongly supported. The original Prop I brought in $200 million per year by taxing the sale of very expensive properties (those worth over $10 million). This revenue has since increased to $240 million/year, and is an excellent means of taxing the rich. Although Greens strongly support the current transfer tax, we did not reach consensus on the new Prop I, which would redirect about half of the money ($120 million/year) to affordable housing run by nonprofits. We therefore did not take a position supporting or opposing Prop I." / "Prop I starts with a mostly revenue-neutral tweak that would raise taxes on the highest value properties while also exempting new development (another example of the control of real estate developers over City politics). But Prop I's major effect would be to require that $120 million/year would be required to be spent on affordable housing run by nonprofits. Some Greens think that such projects are a good use of money and essential to preventing homelessness and displacement. Other Greens argued that the money should be invested in a better affordable housing model instead (such as tenant-governed social housing for people of all income levels), as the non-profit housing model results in poorly run developments and is subject to corruption. Since we did not reach consensus, we hope that individual Greens will weigh both sides and make up your own mind."

subject.title: California — Proposition 2 (Increases State's Rainy Day Fund)

positions.statement: "NO on 2 - put more state tax money in 'rainy day fund' instead of priorities like public transit" / "Prop 2 is also a repeat of a previous bad idea, Prop 2 from 2014. The previous measure changed the maximum size of California's 'rainy day fund' from 5% of annual revenue to 10%, and the new Prop 2 would raise that limit again to 20%. This was a bad idea then and a worse idea now. As we wrote at the time:" / "Unfortunately, our state schools and universities are in a 'rainy day' right now. It is foolish to withhold money rather then spending it at a time when spending is desperately needed to stimulate the economy. The tech sector is doing great, but for most other people, the economy is as bad as it's been since the Wall Street meltdown." / "We should be spending state money on priorities like public transit rather than raising taxes on poor people. Vote NO on Prop 2."
